stories.headline: Supreme Court prepares to rule on Quebec secularism law and Charter rights
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada is set to release its historic decision determining the constitutional validity of Quebec's Bill 21, which prohibits certain public sector workers from wearing religious symbols. The ruling tests the limits of fundamental freedoms under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms as well as the scope of the notwithstanding clause. The outcome carries profound legal consequences for minority rights and national unity across Canada.

stories.headline: Temporary resident population projected to exceed federal target through 2027
stories.summary: Immigration Minister Lena Diab announced that temporary residents are expected to make up 5.5 per cent of Canada's total population by the end of 2027, surpassing the federal ceiling of 5 per cent. The revised outlook reflects ongoing demographic pressures and difficulties in drawing down international student and work permit numbers. The variance will likely heighten parliamentary scrutiny over immigration planning and its impact on public infrastructure.

stories.headline: Federal major projects legislation faces Senate resistance and labour union criticism
stories.summary: The federal government's Bill C-39, designed to expedite regulatory reviews for major infrastructure projects and amend labour standards, is facing pushback ahead of the holiday recess. The Canadian Labour Congress warned that proposed amendments fail to adequately protect workers' constitutional right to strike, while senators and Indigenous leaders raised environmental and consultation concerns. Despite division within caucus and committee opposition, the government maintains that the economic bill will pass.

stories.headline: Quebec legislature will sit without mandatory oath to King despite court ruling
stories.summary: Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon confirmed that the provincial legislature will proceed with its upcoming session without elected members swearing the oath of allegiance to the King. The decision defies a recent court ruling that declared the monarchical oath mandatory under Canada's constitution, an order the province is now appealing. The confrontation establishes a high-stakes legal clash over provincial autonomy and the Crown's role in Canadian democracy.

stories.headline: Conservatives demand parliamentary testimony from Prime Minister's wife on envoy duties
stories.summary: Federal Conservatives are demanding that Diana Fox Carney, wife of Prime Minister Mark Carney, appear before Parliament to testify regarding her role as ocean envoy. Mandate documents show her position involves securing government commitments, leading the opposition to allege a lack of transparency and raise concerns over potential lobbying conflicts. The demand intensifies political scrutiny over ethics and non-civil-service appointments in the prime minister's office.

stories.headline: Suspected North Korean cyber operative secured remote Canadian jobs via false Toronto identity
stories.summary: An investigation has exposed suspected North Korean operatives posing as Canadian citizens through a fraudulent Toronto-based IT business to obtain remote technology positions in domestic corporations and government agencies. The scheme enabled workers to funnel salary earnings back to the sanctioned regime in Pyongyang to evade international financial controls. The findings have raised alarms about background screening failures and national security vulnerabilities within remote working arrangements across Canada.

articles.title: This suspected North Korean operative said he had an IT company in Toronto. It wasn't real

stories.headline: Former oversight member urges police referrals for contentious Ontario MAID cases
stories.summary: A physician and former member of Ontario's assisted dying oversight committee told a parliamentary committee that two medically assisted deaths in the province warranted referral to police. The expert argued that the incidents tested the legal limits of assisted suicide legislation and highlighted risks of coercion among vulnerable individuals. The testimony brings renewed attention to the adequacy of clinical safeguards and the debate surrounding MAID oversight across Canada.

stories.headline: Doug Ford advocates castle law and armed self-defence following violent home invasions
stories.summary: Premier Doug Ford announced that he is a legal firearm owner and would not hesitate to shoot an armed intruder entering his home, urging Ontarians to fight back against home invasions. Ford called for federal Criminal Code amendments to enact castle law protections that allow residents to use whatever force necessary to protect their property and families. The premier's rhetoric has sparked significant controversy regarding vigilante self-defence in the wake of a fatal Toronto break-in.

stories.headline: Ontario and Unifor urge Ottawa to exempt automakers from emissions penalties
stories.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor national president Lana Payne have jointly called on the federal government to eliminate greenhouse gas compliance penalties for Canadian automakers. They argue that federal tailpipe emissions mandates undermine the competitiveness and viability of domestic manufacturing plants during an uncertain transition period. The joint appeal follows recent political tensions and corporate shifts across automotive manufacturing facilities in southern Ontario.

stories.headline: Supreme Court agrees to hear constitutional challenge over Ontario Greenbelt law
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada has agreed to hear an appeal from developer Minotar Holdings challenging Ontario legislation governing the protected Greenbelt. The developer argues that portions of its property were improperly incorporated into the conservation boundary. The decision will set a key judicial precedent on the constitutional boundaries of provincial land planning and development restrictions.

stories.headline: Ontario ministry was warned about private college student aid surge a year earlier
stories.summary: Records reveal that the Ontario government received explicit written warnings over a year ago concerning massive student aid growth at the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology. Although financial aid payouts at the institution skyrocketed by thousands of per cent, the school was excluded from provincial cutoffs applied to six other private career colleges. The revelations have prompted renewed criticism regarding Queen's Park's oversight of public student loans and private post-secondary education.

stories.headline: Ontario mandates driver licences and insurance for motorcycle-style electric bikes
stories.summary: The Ontario government will require drivers of motorcycle- and moped-style electric bikes to obtain licences, vehicle registration, and insurance starting May 1. The new rules aim to address road safety hazards, excessive speeds, and pedestrian safety concerns caused by heavy e-bikes operating in bicycle lanes. The change is set to alter traffic enforcement and micromobility regulations on municipal roads throughout Toronto and across the province.

stories.headline: Public Health Ontario warned government on betting harms as advertising debate grows
stories.summary: Government records indicate Public Health Ontario warned the provincial government about significant public health risks stemming from commercial online sports betting shortly after the sector expanded. Although Premier Doug Ford acknowledged that wagering advertisements have grown out of control, Queen's Park is resisting calls from opposition parties and healthcare groups to ban marketing. Medical professionals report rising emergency room presentations and distress calls connected to gambling addiction across Ontario.

stories.headline: City of Toronto audit reveals questionable staff spending on corporate credit cards
stories.summary: An expenditure analysis revealed that City of Toronto employees used municipal credit cards for hundreds of questionable purchases, including baseball tickets, gift cards, and disputed dating app charges. While city management insists robust auditing checks are active, municipal finance experts argue that internal controls and oversight mechanisms remain inadequate. The spending revelations come at a sensitive time as city council explores revenue-generating measures to bridge significant operating shortfalls.

stories.headline: Toronto proposal for emergency phone fee sparks potential budget clash with Queen's Park
stories.summary: The City of Toronto is exploring new municipal revenue tools, including a proposed $2 monthly fee on mobile phone bills to support 911 dispatch operations. The tax proposal risks provincial intervention, as Premier Doug Ford's government holds statutory authority to overrule municipal taxation measures. The conflicting positions set up a major political clash between Mayor Olivia Chow's administration and the provincial government over municipal finances.
